titre: Hilbert's Problems: Ten Spoken, Twenty-Three Written
accroche: In Paris in 1900, Hilbert presented only ten of his twenty-three problems. A twenty-fourth stayed in his notebook until 2000.
contenu_vulgarise:
In collective memory, David Hilbert stands up in 1900 before the Second International Congress of Mathematicians, in Paris, and states twenty-three problems that will steer a century of research. He presented ten. The historian Rüdiger Thiele recalls this in the *American Mathematical Monthly* in 2003: for lack of time, Hilbert set out only ten problems at the congress.

## A Lecture That No Longer Exists

The complete list appeared only in the fall of 1900, in the *Göttinger Nachrichten*, under the title “Mathematische Probleme.” Mary Winston Newson translated it into English for the *Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society* in 1902. The text of the speech itself has not been preserved, and was never published, writes Thiele. The printed article is, according to him, an expanded version of the speech, written for publication.

Hilbert was preparing this text during a semester in which he was teaching ten hours of classes a week. He had missed a deadline for the congress, so the program sent to participants did not announce his lecture. In mid-July, he surprises his friends Hurwitz and Minkowski by sending them the proofs of the article. Both advise him to shorten his talk, which he accepts: ten problems at the podium, and the rest to the printer.

## The Twenty-Fourth

In his notebooks, Thiele found in 2000 a statement that Hilbert had set aside. It is neither in the speech nor in any printed version, and Hilbert had not communicated it to Hurwitz and Minkowski either. According to Thiele's translation, the notebook says that the twenty-fourth problem was to concern criteria of simplicity, or the proof of the greatest simplicity of certain proofs. Hilbert also writes there that, faced with two proofs of the same theorem, one should keep going until deriving each from the other, or until seeing clearly which conditions and which tools distinguish them.

It is a question about proofs themselves, and not about a mathematical object.

## One List, Two Versions

The printed list displays a conviction: every precise mathematical problem can be settled, either by an answer or by proof of the impossibility of a solution. It is this conviction that the article unfolds, problem after problem, and it does not need all twenty-three to be heard. The version that circulates, that of a speaker stating twenty-three problems before the congress, confuses the abridged lecture with the printed article. When are two proofs of the same theorem two paths, and when only one view seen from two angles?

carte.punch: Hilbert's 23 problems: in Paris in 1900, he presented only ten aloud.
carte.idee: The list of Hilbert's 23 problems appears in the fall of 1900, after the Paris congress. For lack of time, he presented only ten at the podium. A twenty-fourth, on the simplicity of proofs, set aside from the list, was found in his notebooks only in 2000, by Rüdiger Thiele.

quiz.question: How many problems did Hilbert present aloud at the Paris congress, and why?
choix: All twenty-three, read in full before the congress
Fifteen, eight others having been added after remarks from participants
None: the congress had refused his lecture, and he published the text alone
Ten, for lack of time, after Hurwitz and Minkowski advised him to shorten it
quiz.explication: According to Thiele, Hilbert presented ten problems, his friends Hurwitz and Minkowski having advised him to shorten the talk; the complete list of twenty-three then appears in the Göttinger Nachrichten. It was not read in full, problems were not added after the fact by participants, and the lecture was not refused, only absent from the announced program.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What was Hilbert's twenty-fourth problem, which remained unpublished, about?
choix: Criteria of simplicity for mathematical proofs
The existence of a general solution to all polynomial equations
The consistency of arithmetic, taken up later by Gödel
The classification of finite simple groups
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to Thiele, Hilbert's notebook describes the twenty-fourth problem as concerning criteria of simplicity for proofs, and not the consistency of arithmetic, the existence of polynomial solutions, or the classification of groups, which are not mentioned in that notebook.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where was the complete list of Hilbert's twenty-three problems first published?
choix: In the printed proceedings of the Paris congress
In an open letter to the participants of the congress
In the Göttinger Nachrichten, in the fall of 1900
In the Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society, in 1900
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The complete list of twenty-three problems appeared only in the fall of 1900 in the Göttinger Nachrichten, the speech itself never having been published, and Newson's translation in the Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society dates from 1902, not 1900.
